name: Pedro Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the department office for Earth Sciences at the university, so about forty staff and a couple of hundred students. Mornings are room bookings, exam timetables and expense claims; the professors send me receipts photographed on a car bonnet in the rain. Afternoons are filing, minutes for meetings, and answering students who've lost their login.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person who knows how things work, like which form gets a field trip insured. What wears me out is the expense claims, honestly. I've started using the AI chat tool the university pays for to tidy up meeting minutes, maybe twice a week, but I check every line because it once invented an apology from the Head of Department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's sort of my working theory already, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter, like the fact that the university pays cleaners less than it pays the coffee machine lease. At work I'd say the minutes tool saves me an hour a week and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty relaxed. I've got a permanent contract, the union's strong at the university, and departments always need someone to chase receipts. The thing that bothers me in that world is rent, not robots: Lina and I pay a lot for a small flat near the hospital where she works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and use the minutes tool when it helps. I'd go to the union's pay meetings, because the pay offer this year was below prices. And Lina and I would keep putting about £250 a month aside for a deposit, which we've done since last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. A bit flat, maybe, because all the excitement turned out to be nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the minutes tool saves an hour a week. What do you do with that hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gets eaten by expense claims. Professor Adeyemi alone sends me about thirty receipts a month, half of them in a language I don't read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you worried in that picture, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the university had a bad year for student numbers. They've already talked about a hiring freeze. Nobody gets fired, people just aren't replaced, and that's how admin jobs disappear at a university.

say: AI saves me about **an hour a week** on minutes, and that's all.
The real issues are **low pay** for cleaners and rent, not robots.
think: A **permanent contract** and a strong union make me feel secure here.
**Rent** for our small flat near the hospital is the real pressure.
do: Keep using the **minutes tool** only when it actually helps.
Go to the union's **pay meetings** about this year's low offer.
Keep saving **£250 a month** with Lina towards a deposit.
feel: Fine, a bit **flat**, because the excitement came to nothing.
S0.quote: Nobody gets fired, people just aren't replaced, and that's how admin jobs disappear at a university.
fieldNote: He feels **secure** thanks to a permanent contract and a strong union.
He names the **hiring freeze** as the quiet way admin jobs vanish.
His AI use is **careful and limited**, after the tool once invented an apology.

steps.text: Keep using the university AI tool for meeting minutes
Go to union meetings about this year's pay offer
Save £250 a month with Lina towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's closer to what I'm already seeing, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union branch that we need a technology agreement now: no job losses without consultation, and retraining paid in work time. I'd probably write a post about it for the staff newsletter. Publicly I'd be fair about it, because some of the tools really do help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the department office goes from three of us to one or two. Expenses, room booking, student queries: that's all on the card. I'm average at the job, not the best, and the woman who runs the finance side, Ruth, is really sharp, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get properly good at the AI tools the university already has, so I'm the one who sets them up, not the one they replace. I'd ask about the research administration course the university runs, which is about managing grant money, because grant rules are complicated and someone has to own them. And we'd pause the deposit plan for a few months and keep the cash liquid instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. More like before an exam I've half revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why research administration in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because grants come with pages of rules, and when something goes wrong a real person signs to say it's correct. I'd rather be the one signing than the one typing it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some tools really help, but you're also pushing the union hard. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I like the AI tools, I just don't trust the people deciding how many of us they need afterwards. Liking the hammer doesn't mean you trust the man swinging it.

say: The union needs a **technology agreement**: consultation first, retraining in work time.
Some tools **really help**, and I'd say so fairly in the staff newsletter.
think: The department office probably shrinks from **three people** to one or two.
I'm **average**, and Ruth on the finance side is sharper than me.
do: Get good enough at the **AI tools** to be the one setting them up.
Ask about the **research administration course** on managing grant money.
Pause the **deposit plan** and keep savings easy to reach.
feel: Nervous but **not hopeless**, like an exam I've half revised for.
S1.quote: I like the AI tools, I just don't trust the people deciding how many of us they need afterwards.
fieldNote: He expects **cuts in his office** and ranks himself honestly against a colleague.
He holds two views at once: **likes the tools**, distrusts the bosses.
His move is towards **grant administration**, where a person still signs off.

steps.text: Learn to set up the university's AI tools for the office
Take the university's research administration course on grants
Push the union branch for a technology agreement
Pause the deposit plan and keep cash easy to reach

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. By 2028. That's two more academic years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when governments are supposed to act: shorter working weeks, a basic income, a tax on the AI companies. I'd go to the demonstrations and I'd sign everything. At work I'd tell people to keep their union membership up, because a union with no members can't negotiate anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think university admin is finished by 2029. If AI can do almost any thinking work, it can do the grants course I was going to take, too. Robots coming three years later doesn't save me, because nothing I do needs hands except the photocopier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Lina that week and work out how long our savings last on her pay alone, which is about four months of my share. I'd look seriously at nursing or healthcare assistant work at her hospital, because that's hands-on and gets the extra three years. And I'd stop the deposit plan completely and keep every penny in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. And a bit angry that the people building this didn't ask anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Lina's nursing job in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the strange bit: her job's safer than mine for a while, because the robots come later. So for the first time she'd be the one carrying us, and I'd have to get okay with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really retrain as a healthcare assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. I did a summer in a care home at eighteen and I wasn't bad at it. The pay's worse than mine now, but worse pay beats no pay.

say: Governments must act with **shorter weeks**, basic income and an AI tax.
Keep your **union membership** up, because an empty union can't negotiate.
think: University admin is **finished by 2029**, grants work included.
The **three-year robot gap** doesn't help a job that only touches a photocopier.
do: Work out with Lina how long savings last on **her pay alone**.
Apply for **healthcare assistant** work at Lina's hospital.
Stop the **deposit plan** and keep every penny in the bank.
feel: Scared, and **angry** that nobody was asked.
S2.quote: Robots coming three years later doesn't save me, because nothing I do needs hands except the photocopier.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** and sees even his planned retraining wiped out.
He'd lean on his partner's **nursing income**, a role reversal he's still getting used to.
His hands-on fallback comes from a **care home summer** at eighteen.

steps.text: Work out with Lina how long savings last on her pay
Apply for healthcare assistant jobs at Lina's hospital
Stop the flat deposit plan and keep the cash
Join demonstrations for an AI tax and basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that gives me a bit of room to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but I'd add that five years is enough to do this properly: retraining paid for by the employer, notice periods that mean something. I'd want the university to be the good example, since it's always telling everyone else how to behave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I keep my job for two or three years and then it goes. That's actually useful, because it's the time I'd need to train for something else while still being paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start an evening course towards healthcare assistant work, or maybe the first year of a nursing degree if I can get funding. I'd keep using the AI tools at work, because being useful buys me time. We'd still save for a flat but in a cheaper town nearer Lina's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. A plan makes most things feel smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why closer to Lina's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a big house and her dad keeps offering us the downstairs. If I'm a student at 30 we'll need cheap rent, and pride doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your job for two or three years. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Universities move slowly, everything goes through committees, and here that's two years of salary. That's normally what drives me mad, but this time it works for me.

say: Five years is enough to do this **properly**, with paid retraining and real notice.
The university should be the **good example** it keeps telling others to be.
think: I keep the job for about **two or three years**, then it goes.
That gap is **paid time** to train for something else.
do: Start an **evening course** towards healthcare assistant or nursing work.
Keep using the **AI tools** at work to stay useful.
Save for a flat in a **cheaper town** near Lina's parents.
feel: Uneasy, but a **plan** makes it feel smaller.
S3.quote: Universities move slowly, everything goes through committees, and here that's two years of salary.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the job**, but sees the delay as paid training time.
He finds a silver lining in **slow committees**, which usually annoy him.
Family help from **Lina's parents** is part of his plan.

steps.text: Start an evening course towards healthcare assistant work
Keep using AI tools at work to stay useful
Save for a flat in a cheaper town near Lina's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to build something fair, and if we don't, that's a political choice. I'd talk about it at union meetings and at dinner with Lina's family, who all vote differently from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the people who does fine, as long as I start early. The danger is that ten years makes everyone lazy, including me, and the admin cuts still come years before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short course on research grants and data, and use the AI tools more at work. Around year three I'd decide between grants and nursing, depending on how the tools look. We'd buy a flat sooner rather than later, while I've still got a steady salary for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. There's still a background hum of worry, but it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the bank wants to see a steady salary, and in ten years I might be a student or changing jobs. Get the mortgage while I still look boring on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want kids in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in four or five years. Lina wants two, I want one, so we'll end up with two.

say: A decade is time to **build something fair**, and failing would be a choice.
I'd argue it at **union meetings** and with Lina's family.
think: I'll **do fine** if I start early.
Ten years makes people **lazy**, and admin cuts still come early.
do: Take a **short course** on research grants and data in year one.
Decide between **grants or nursing** around year three.
Buy a flat **soon**, while a steady salary gets a mortgage.
feel: Mostly okay, with a quiet **background hum** of worry.
S4.quote: Get the mortgage while I still look boring on paper.
fieldNote: He sees himself **coming out fine**, which is why the mood eases.
He spots the risk of **complacency**, including his own.
His **mortgage timing** shows practical thinking about how banks see job changes.

steps.text: Take a short course on research grants and data
Buy a flat while a steady salary gets a mortgage
Use the university AI tools more in daily work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to be paid while I retrain. What would help is a proper retraining wage, like getting paid a basic salary to study nursing, and a union that's actually at the table when they decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks about my job, but what keeps me calm in all of these is that Lina's job lasts longer than mine.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but what keeps me calm in all of these is that Lina's job lasts longer than mine.
portrait: Pedro, 27, runs the **Earth Sciences** department office at a university and lives with Lina, a nurse.
He uses the university's AI tool **now and then**, and checks every line it writes.
He's a committed **union member** who likes the tools but distrusts how bosses use them.
In the fast AGI picture he expects to **lose his job** and lean on Lina's income.
With more time he plans **healthcare or grants work**, and buying a flat early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no paid time to retrain before his job goes.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining wage** to study something like nursing.
A **union at the table** when decisions about jobs are made.
